The Work and Torah Thought of Rabbi David Oppenheim: His Life, His Famous Library and His Halakhic Method
In a historical setting marked by social, political and cultural transformations in the Holy Roman Empire of the early modern period, the figure of Rabbi David Oppenheim (Maharar David Oppenheim; 5424–7 Tishrei 5497, 1664–1736) stands out as a canonical figure without precedent [cite: 1]. Serving as av beit din and mara d'atra (local halakhic authority) in the central communities of Nikolsburg and Prague, and as chief rabbi of the state of Bohemia on behalf of the imperial government, Rabbi David embodied the ideal of "Torah and greatness in one place" at its zenith [cite: 1, 2, 3]. His life's work extended across firm halakhic leadership, original rulings in the responsa "Nish'al David," the establishment of a far-reaching network of ties with the leading Court Jews, and the creation of the largest and most important surviving collection of Hebrew books and manuscripts of the early modern period [cite: 1, 4, 5]. This library, which served in his lifetime as a center of knowledge and a source of Torah and public authority, is today housed in the Bodleian Library at the University of Oxford and continues to be a central foundation for bibliographical and historical research [cite: 4, 6].
His Life, Lineage and Political-Social Standing
Rabbi David Oppenheim was born in the month of Sivan 5424 (June 1664) in the city of Worms (Vermaiza) in Germany, one of the long-established centers of Ashkenazi Torah and culture [cite: 1, 7]. He was born to Rabbi Avraham Oppenheim, of a distinguished and very wealthy family whose ties were joined to the dynasties of wealth and influence of the "Court Jews" in the Holy Roman Empire [cite: 1, 2, 8]. His uncle was the renowned negid (Jewish leader), Rabbi Shmuel Oppenheimer, financial manager and chief purveyor of the imperial court in Vienna [cite: 1, 8]. Oppenheimer's connections with Prince Eugene of Savoy yielded, among other things, a wealth of rare Hebrew manuscripts that were brought from the Ottoman Empire after the Great Turkish War and passed to Rabbi David [cite: 1, 8].
In his youth Rabbi David married Gnendel, daughter of the Court Jew Lipmann Katz (Leffmann Behrends) of Hanover [cite: 1, 5]. This marriage strengthened his economic standing and gave him complete financial independence, which allowed him to devote his life to Torah study, to the management of communities and to the acquisition of books, without dependence on communal sources of livelihood [cite: 6, 7]. After the death of his wife Gnendel, he married a second time the daughter of Rabbi Binyamin Wolf Shapira, av beit din of Prague, a family bond that connected him deeply to the leadership of the community in Bohemia [cite: 2, 9].
Already in his youth Rabbi David stood out as an exceptional Torah prodigy. At about the age of 20 he received rabbinic ordination, and at the age of 25 only (in the month of Elul 5449, 1689) he was appointed rabbi of Nikolsburg and mara d'atra of the state of Moravia (Landesrabbiner) [cite: 1, 2, 5]. During his twenty years of service in Nikolsburg he established his standing as one of the great halakhic decisors of his generation, with the sages of Europe sending him complex halakhic questions and seeking his approbations for their books [cite: 1, 2]. In 5462 (1702) he moved to Prague, and in 5472 (1712) he was appointed chief rabbi of the city of Prague and the districts of Bohemia [cite: 2, 5, 10]. Prague was at that time one of the largest and most central Jewish communities in Europe, and his tenure there lasted about 24 years, until his death on 7 Tishrei 5497 (12 September 1736) at the age of 72 [cite: 1]. He was laid to rest in the old Jewish cemetery of Prague [cite: 1].
The standing of Rabbi David Oppenheim went far beyond the bounds of the classical rabbinic office. Thanks to his extensive ties with the emperor's court in Vienna and to his family lineage, he served as an intercessor and as a defender of the rights of the Jews in the kingdom, and the imperial government granted him an official letter of appointment as chief rabbi of the entire state of Bohemia, a position that gave him broad judicial and administrative powers [cite: 1, 2]. Alongside his activity in Europe, Rabbi David headed the efforts to support the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, and coordinated the apparatus for collecting funds and transferring economic support to the yeshivot and sages of Jerusalem, Safed and Hebron [cite: 3, 10]. In recognition of his decisive support and of his standing as the spiritual and material father of the Jews of the Land of Israel, the sages of Jerusalem bestowed on him the exalted honorific "Nasi of the Land of Israel" (or "Nasi of Israel") [cite: 1, 3, 10]. Rabbi David printed copies of the letter of appointment he received from the emissaries of Jerusalem and distributed them, as part of establishing his all-Israel authority [cite: 11].

His Teachers, Torah Ties and Network of Influence
Rabbi David Oppenheim grew up in the magnificent study halls of Ashkenaz and France in the 17th century, and his Torah education combined the long-established Ashkenazi learning traditions with the new talmudic analysis that developed in Central Europe. His foremost teacher in his youth was Rabbi Gershon Ashkenazi (author of the responsa "Avodat HaGershuni"), who served as rabbi in the city of Metz [cite: 1, 2, 10]. From him Rabbi David received the method of fundamental and practical halakhic analysis. In addition, he studied with Rabbi Yitzchak Binyamin Wolf of Landsberg (author of "Nachalat Binyamin"), who was one of the great teachers in Ashkenaz and deeply influenced his manner of study and of rendering rulings [cite: 1, 2]. Later he deepened his learning with Rabbi Yaakov Z"K Ashkenazi (father of Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Ashkenazi, the "Chacham Tzvi"), study that laid the foundation for his friendship with the great men of the generation, and with Rabbi Binyamin Wolf Epstein in the city of Friedberg, with whom he completed his course of study before being appointed to the rabbinate [cite: 1].
The Torah and social network of Rabbi David was among the most extensive and influential in Europe. Already in his youth he formed a deep friendship with Rabbi Yair Chaim Bacharach (author of the responsa "Chavot Yair"), and maintained a rich Torah correspondence with him [cite: 1, 5]. His family ties wove him together with the leading figures of the Torah world of his generation. Rabbi Yaakov Reischer (author of "Shevut Yaakov") was his brother-in-law, and in his books addressed Rabbi David in terms of exalted praise and admiration, such as "my beloved, my lord, my brother-in-law, the great gaon, famed in every corner and region... glory of the generation" and "Rabban of the Diaspora" [cite: 1, 10]. His renowned son-in-law, who married his daughter, was Rabbi Chaim Yonah Teomim (author of "Kuntres R. Chaim Yonah"), one of the great scholars and decisors in Prague [cite: 1, 2, 10]. He was also a family connection of Rabbi Yonatan Eybeschutz during the latter's stay in Prague [cite: 9]. His only son, Rabbi Yosef Oppenheim, who served as av beit din of Alsace, married the daughter of the famous Court Jew Rabbi Shimshon Wertheimer of Vienna, thereby uniting the two most powerful families of leadership and wealth in European Jewry [cite: 1, 2]. This network served as a vital channel for the transfer of halakhic information, books and manuscripts, and for the coordination of communal and political policy throughout the empire [cite: 7, 11].
The Oppenheim Library – "Prince of the Press" and the Treasure of the Hebrew Book
The central achievement of Rabbi David Oppenheim, which fixed his place in the pages of the cultural history of the Jewish people, is the collection of books and manuscripts he established [cite: 4, 5]. In a world in which books were a precious and extremely rare commodity, Rabbi David invested his enormous fortune in creating the most comprehensive bibliographical collection of early modern Hebrew literature [cite: 6, 12].
Already at the age of 22, in 1686, Rabbi David began to catalogue his private collection, which then numbered about 400 titles – a tremendous achievement considering that in the whole world only about 2,000 Hebrew titles had been printed until then [cite: 7]. At the age of 24 the collection numbered 480 books [cite: 13], and at its peak it expanded to giant dimensions of about 750 to 780 rare manuscripts and about 4,220 to 4,500 printed books [cite: 4, 14, 15]. This collection encompassed all fields of Jewish creativity: Bible, Talmud, halakha, Kabbalah, philosophy, prayer books (mahzorim), homiletics, poetry and early Yiddish literature [cite: 7, 14].
The methods of acquisition and collecting of Rabbi David were planned and complex. He dispatched agents and emissaries throughout Europe, the Balkans and the Land of Israel in order to locate rare books [cite: 12]. At the same time, he kept a series of private scribes and copyists, such as the scribe Azriel of Krotoszyn, who copied for him dozens of works and rare manuscripts that could not be purchased [cite: 11]. Moreover, Rabbi David financed many printers in Europe and supplied them with fine, high-quality paper (and sometimes even parchment) so that they would print for him unique copies (deluxe copies) [cite: 1]. Thanks to this, there survive in his library unique copies in the world of books and pamphlets all of whose other copies were lost [cite: 1, 14]. To mark his ownership, he developed an elaborate personal bookplate (Ex-Libris), and made use of royal symbols and biblical figures, in particular King David, to express the conception of the "crown of Torah" combined with leadership [cite: 7].
Prague, which was under Habsburg rule and the strong Catholic influence of the Jesuit Order, suffered from severe censorship and the confiscation of Hebrew books [cite: 13]. As rabbi of the community, Rabbi David understood that the judgments and bans of the imperial censorship could endanger his precious collection [cite: 13]. He therefore took an extraordinary strategic step and stored his entire enormous library in the city of Hanover, in the house of his father-in-law Lipmann Katz, which was protected under the Protestant principality of Hanover [cite: 1, 16]. Throughout his life as rabbi in Prague, his library stood hundreds of kilometers from him. Rabbi David used to travel frequently to Hanover to consult his books, and he made use of messengers and scribes who brought him specific manuscripts according to his study and halakhic needs [cite: 10, 11].
After his death in 1736, the library passed into the ownership of his son Rabbi Yosef, and afterwards to his granddaughter and her husband, who lived in Hildesheim [cite: 2, 11]. The family sank into debt and used the library as collateral for loans [cite: 11]. For decades the library stood for sale, and sums far below its estimated value were offered for it (original estimate: 150,000 thalers) [cite: 5]. In 1829 the collection was purchased in its entirety by the Bodleian Library at the University of Oxford for the sum of 2,080 pounds sterling (about 9,000 thalers) [cite: 4, 5]. This purchase at one stroke doubled Oxford's collection of Hebrew manuscripts and made it one of the most important world centers for Jewish studies [cite: 4]. The scholars of the "Chokhmat Yisrael" in Europe, headed by Leopold Zunz, lamented the departure of the treasure beyond the borders of the Jewish center in Europe, but thanks to this purchase the collection has been preserved intact to this day [cite: 5]. The modern scholar Joshua Teplitsky dedicated to the library and to the work of Rabbi David his comprehensive book Prince of the Press (2019) [cite: 7, 11, 17, 18].

His Torah Enterprise, Writings and Halakhic Method
Alongside being a book collector and a public leader, Rabbi David Oppenheim was a first-rank halakhic decisor and a Torah innovator [cite: 1]. He composed about twenty books on halakha, aggadah and exegesis, but in his humility – and out of a striving to reach perfection and the utmost precision – he did not print most of his works in his lifetime, and they remained in manuscript [cite: 1, 2]. Rabbi David used to give his books names containing his own name ("David") [cite: 2].

The halakhic rulings of Rabbi David Oppenheim are characterized by a fusion of classical Ashkenazi scholarship with a deep public vision and social responsibility. He did not regard halakha as merely abstract casuistry, but as a practical instrument for leading the community and for safeguarding the rights of the needy.
One of the famous rulings that illustrate his halakhic method deals with the law of the divorce of a woman who has become insane (a shoteh) [cite: 21]. The gaon Rabbi Naftali Katz (av beit din of Posen and Frankfurt) ruled that it is permitted to have a get (bill of divorce) acquired on behalf of a woman who is a "complete shoteh," so that she would be considered unmarried, on the conception that this is a "benefit" for her, to be divorced [cite: 21]. Rabbi David Oppenheim came out forcefully against this permission, and ruled in the responsa "Nish'al David" (Even HaEzer, section 33) that such a get is void by Torah law [cite: 21]. In his legal analysis he determined that a get cannot be taken from a woman who is a shoteh, since she cannot safeguard her get nor herself, and by Torah law she has no capacity for acquisition (zekhiyah) or hand (yad), and therefore the get does not take effect [cite: 21]. Alongside the formal argument, Rabbi David raised a normative value-based and social reasoning: if they divorce a shoteh woman, the environment will treat her as unmarried, and this will lead to abandoning her and treating her with "a manner of ownerlessness" [cite: 21]. This analysis combines rigorous legal analysis with the defense of the weak in society. This ruling was later supported by his brother-in-law, Rabbi Yaakov Reischer, and by the author of the book "Panim Meirot," and became a cornerstone in the laws of marriage [cite: 21].
Another example of his principled stance occurred in 1715, when the Habsburg authorities in Prague attempted to compel Rabbi David Oppenheim to serve as the official censor of all the Hebrew books printed in the city, in order to ensure that they contained nothing against Christianity [cite: 13]. Rabbi David refused firmly and shrewdly to fill this role, and in his official reply to the authorities argued that, because of his advanced age, his weak eyesight and the burden of his rabbinic duties, he was unable to examine the books [cite: 13]. Behind this diplomatic explanation stood a deep halakhic and public conception: Rabbi David refused to turn the rabbinic seat into an arm of government censorship, knowing that agreeing to this would place upon him criminal and religious responsibility for every printed word and would harm the freedom of Jewish study and printing [cite: 13].
His Students, Torah Patronage and Legacy for the Generations
In Prague Rabbi David headed a large yeshiva that drew hundreds of young men and married scholars from all over Ashkenaz and Poland [cite: 2, 11]. He made use of his private library as an extraordinary pedagogical aid: during his daily lessons he used to bring before his students rare manuscripts and ancient printed editions of the Talmud and of the decisors in order to clarify precise textual versions and to examine the development of halakha [cite: 11]. Students and scholars from all over Europe approached him by letter to receive permission to come and consult the manuscripts in his possession for the purpose of writing their books [cite: 11].
The great wealth of Rabbi David served as a central fund of support for the world of the Hebrew book, and many authors who suffered from dire poverty found with him a warm home and full financing for the printing of their books [cite: 2, 20]. A prominent example of this patronage is his support of the kabbalist Rabbi Moshe of Prague, author of the kabbalistic work "Vayakhel Moshe" [cite: 1]. Rabbi David hosted Rabbi Moshe in his home, supported him for years and enabled him to write and print his book without worries of livelihood [cite: 1]. In addition, the approbations of Rabbi David for books were regarded as a first-rate seal of quality, and authors sent him their manuscripts in order to earn his approbation, which assured the book's circulation [cite: 2].
The legacy of Rabbi David Oppenheim extends along several main axes of influence. First, the gathering and management of his collection prevented the loss of hundreds of unique manuscripts and ancient printings, which today constitute the core of the Hebrew collection in the Bodleian Library at Oxford [cite: 4, 14]. Second, his rulings in the responsa "Nish'al David" and in his manuscripts continue to serve as a source of authority for decisors in recent generations, in particular in complex issues of Even HaEzer and Choshen Mishpat [cite: 21]. Finally, his model of leadership represented the peak of Court Jewry: Rabbi David proved that wealth and influence in royal courts can directly serve the fortification of the Torah world, the strengthening of communities and the defense of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel [cite: 3, 8, 10, 12].
Summary and Conclusions
The figure of Rabbi David Oppenheim stands as one of the pillars of the culture of the book and of Jewish leadership in the transition from the early modern period to the modern period [cite: 7, 11]. The combination of his economic, family and political circumstances, together with his diligence in Torah and his halakhic genius, enabled him to create a life's work of historic dimensions [cite: 1, 3, 6].
His enormous library was not the amusement of a wealthy collector, but a strategic instrument for leadership, research and halakhic rulings [cite: 7, 12]. Through the mechanism of acquisition, copying and preservation that he created, Rabbi David established a center of knowledge that linked the sages of Ashkenaz, Sepharad and the Land of Israel [cite: 7, 12]. His considered decision to store his collections in Hanover became a model of strategic planning in the face of religious and imperial censorship [cite: 13, 16]. Today, when the manuscripts and books of Rabbi David Oppenheim are studied in yeshivot and universities alike, his name is engraved not only as "Rabban of the Diaspora" and as "Nasi of the Land of Israel," but also as the "Prince of the Press" who rescued and preserved the memory of the Hebrew written word for the generations [cite: 1, 3, 7].
